deep.reconstruction:
This page is the fair copy of p.4 of Riemann's 1859 Monatsberichte paper 'Ueber die Anzahl der Primzahlen unter einer gegebenen Grösse'. It runs from the definition of F(x) to the start of the explicit formula.

(1) Normalisation at jumps. F(x) = pi(x) when x is not a prime. At a jump, F(x) = (F(x+0)+F(x-0))/2.

(2) Dirichlet series as a Mellin integral. Take the logarithm of the Euler product:
log zeta(s) = -Sum_p log(1-p^{-s}) = Sum_p Sum_n (1/n) p^{-ns}.
Use p^{-ns} = s * Int_{p^n}^oo x^{-s-1} dx for Re s > 0. Summing over p and n and exchanging sum and integral (absolutely convergent for Re s > 1) gives
log zeta(s)/s = Int_1^oo f(x) x^{-s-1} dx,
where f(x) = Sum_n (1/n) F(x^{1/n}). This f is the modern Riemann prime-counting function J(x) = Pi_0(x). The identity is valid for s = a+bi with a > 1.

(3) Fourier inversion, i.e. Mellin inversion. Suppose g(s) = Int_0^oo h(x) x^{-s} dlog x for Re s = a > 1, with h real. Write g(a+bi) = g1(b) + i g2(b). Then
- g1(b) = Int h x^{-a} cos(b log x) dlog x;
- i g2(b) = -i Int h x^{-a} sin(b log x) dlog x.
Multiply by e^{i b log y} db and integrate over b from -oo to oo. By Fourier's integral theorem each gives pi h(y) y^{-a}, so the sum gives 2 pi h(y) y^{-a}. Multiplying by i y^a and putting s = a+bi (so ds = i db):
2 pi i h(y) = Int_{a-i oo}^{a+i oo} g(s) y^s ds,
with the integration taken along Re s = a constant. At a jump of h the integral gives the mean of the two one-sided values. f was normalised to have exactly this property, so for all y:
f(y) = (1/2 pi i) Int_{(a)} (log zeta(s)/s) y^s ds.
This is the Perron/Mellin inversion formula.

(4) Substituting the product formula. From p.3, with xi(t) = Pi(s/2)(s-1) pi^{-s/2} zeta(s), s = 1/2 + it, and the Hadamard-type product xi(t) = xi(0) Prod(1 - tt/alpha alpha):
log zeta(s) = (s/2) log pi - log(s-1) - log Pi(s/2) + Sum_alpha log(1 + (s-1/2)^2/alpha^2) + log xi(0).
Integrated term by term along the vertical line, the individual integrals would not converge. Riemann therefore first integrates by parts (boundary terms dropped, unproved):
f(x) = -(1/2 pi i)(1/log x) Int_{(a)} d/ds[log zeta(s)/s] x^s ds.

(5) The Gamma term. Gauss's product Pi(x) = lim_{m->oo} m! m^x / Prod_{n=1}^m (x+n) gives
-log Pi(s/2) = lim_m [Sum_{n<=m} log(1+s/(2n)) - (s/2) log m].
After dividing by s, the term (s/2) log m becomes a constant and is killed by d/ds. Hence
-d/ds[(1/s) log Pi(s/2)] = Sum_{n>=1} d/ds[(1/s) log(1+s/(2n))].
Therefore every term of the expression for f(x) has the form ±(1/2 pi i)(1/log x) Int d/ds[(1/s) log(1-s/beta)] x^s ds (continued on p.5). The one exception is the constant term. Its integrand is (1/s^2) log xi(0); I have checked the sign. Since (1/2 pi i) Int_{(a)} x^s/s^2 ds = log x for x > 1, that term contributes exactly log xi(0).
errors: Riemann says that each of the two equations separately gives pi h(y) y^{-a} after Fourier integration. For general h on (0,oo), the cosine part gives pi[H(v)+H(-v)] and the sine part gives pi[H(v)-H(-v)], where v = log y. So each is pi h(y) y^{-a} only after combination, or when h vanishes for x<1. That second condition holds for f, which is zero below x=2, when y>1. The sum 2 pi h(y) y^{-a} is correct in general. This is a minor imprecision, not an error in the result.
The inversion integral converges only conditionally, as a symmetric limit b->oo. Validity of Fourier's theorem for the jump function f is asserted, not proved.
In the partial integration the boundary terms at a ± i oo are dropped without justification. They do vanish, since log zeta(s)/s -> 0 on Re s = a > 1, but Riemann does not argue this.
Term-by-term handling of the infinite sums over alpha and n is not justified here. Riemann's later remark about conditional convergence of the sum over roots acknowledges the issue.
